chunks.text: In short

Google has indexed Instagram captions since twenty twenty-four and the in-app search bar handles 40% of restaurant discovery for guests under 35; almost no independent restaurant writes captions like it.

Five caption-level moves: the first nine words carry the keyword load, name the dish/cuisine/neighborhood, write for the search query not the photo, hashtags inside the sentence not stacked, fill the alt-text field every time.

Running the discipline on a real DMV account delivered 4.3x the saves and 2.1x the profile clicks vs the same restaurant’s old grid — saves and profile clicks are the only Instagram metrics that correlate with reservations.
Op-ed · May 11, twenty twenty-six · 7 min read · By Don Goldstein

Google has indexed Instagram captions since twenty twenty-four. The in-app search bar handles 40% of restaurant discovery for guests under 35. TikTok’s “search” tab is now the second-most-used surface on the platform. None of this is news. What’s strange is how few independent restaurants have stopped posting like it’s twenty nineteen and started writing for the search bar. The five moves below are what change.

The instinct to treat Instagram as a billboard is hard to kill. You take a nice photo, you write a sentence about your plate, you hit post, and you wait for the engagement signal. Engagement was the right signal in twenty eighteen. It’s not the right signal now. In twenty twenty-six the post is a search-result candidate. The audience isn’t your followers — it’s the person who types “best omakase silver spring” into the in-app search bar and reads the first three captions that come up.

I run two DMV restaurant accounts. One is treated the old way — pretty pictures, vibe captions, hashtags at the bottom. The other is treated as an S E O surface. Same kitchen, same photography budget, posted at the same cadence. The S E O-treated account does 4.3x the saves and 2.1x the profile clicks. Saves and profile clicks are the only Instagram metrics that correlate with reservations. Likes do not.
Why the platform changed and almost nobody noticed.

Two things happened around mid-twenty twenty-four. Meta started exposing post captions to the public web crawl — you can verify this with a Google site:instagram.com query for any restaurant; their captions are indexed. And the in-app search algorithm shifted from ranking by engagement to ranking by content-match. A caption that contained the exact phrase the user searched outranked a caption with the same topic phrased differently, regardless of how many likes it had.

The combined effect: every caption is now competing in two search markets at once. One is Google’s, the other is Instagram’s. The keywords that get you found are slightly different in each, but the writing moves are the same.
The five caption-level moves.

Five caption-level moves that make a restaurant Instagram post discoverable in search, ranked by impact. Move one: the first nine words carry the keyword load. Instagram truncates captions at 125 characters on the feed; if your dish name and city are not in the first nine words, the post will not surface in search. Move two: name the dish, the cuisine, and the neighborhood in plain language. 'Sea bass crudo' beats 'tonight's special'; 'Silver Spring Italian' beats 'come visit us'. Move three: write for the search query, not the photo. The caption answers what someone might have typed, not what the image already shows. Move four: hashtags go inside the caption sentence, not stacked at the bottom. The Instagram algorithm now penalizes hashtag stacks as low-quality content. Move five: alt-text is searchable. Fill in the actual alt-text field on every post; ninety percent of restaurant accounts skip this and surrender the search surface for free.
Move 1: The first nine words carry the keyword load.

Instagram truncates the caption at roughly 125 characters on the feed and search-result pages. That’s about nine to fifteen words depending on word length. After the truncation, “more” appears, and most readers don’t tap it. The keyword density in the first nine words is what the algorithm ranks; it’s also what the human reader actually sees. Bury the dish name in the third sentence and the post is invisible.
The discipline is simple and brutal: write the caption from the search box backwards. What would the guest type? Type that, then add the human flourish after. Not the other way around.
Move 2: Name the dish, the cuisine, the neighborhood.

Three entities, every caption. The dish (specific, not category). The cuisine or genre. The neighborhood or city. “Pici al ragù at Roma Cucina, Silver Spring Italian” is fifteen syllables of pure entity match. The vibe goes after. The platform doesn’t rank on vibe; it ranks on entities.

The reason this feels uncomfortable is that restaurant marketing taught operators for fifteen years that the caption is supposed to evoke the experience. The caption is supposed to do that, eventually. But before it can evoke the experience to a follower, it has to surface to a stranger searching for a meal. The entities are the surfacing layer. The evocation comes after.
The before / after.

Same dish, same restaurant, two captions side by side. The twenty nineteen-style caption: 'Tonight, we are so excited to share something special. Our chef has been working on this for weeks. Come in and let us know what you think. Made with love.' That caption has no dish name, no cuisine, no location, no searchable entity, and the first nine words contain only emotional language. Probability of surfacing on search, near zero. The twenty twenty-six-style caption: 'Pici al ragù, hand-rolled, Tuesday dinner at Roma Cucina — Silver Spring Italian on Georgia Ave. Made with the same recipe my grandmother used in Marche. Reservations open.' That caption names the dish twice, the cuisine, the city, and the street, all in the first thirty characters. It also includes alt-text-friendly description and ends with a soft C T A. Probability of surfacing on search, high.
Move 3: Write for the search query, not the photo.

This is the move that takes the longest to internalize. The photo already shows the dish. The caption’s job is not to describe it — the caption’s job is to answer the search query that brought someone to the post. “Where do I get carbonara in Silver Spring” is a search query. “Carbonara at Roma Cucina, Silver Spring Italian, 24 dollars, Tuesday through Sunday” is the caption that answers it.
The test: cover the photo with your hand and read the caption. Does it stand alone as a search result? If yes, you’ve done move 3. If you have to look at the photo for context, you haven’t.
Move 4: Hashtags inside the sentence, not stacked.

Instagram’s late-twenty twenty-four algorithm update started treating stacked hashtags — the wall of fifteen tags at the bottom of every post — as a low-quality signal. The platform now ranks two or three hashtags placed mid-sentence higher than fifteen stacked at the end. The reason is anti-spam: stacked hashtags were a marker for content farms, so the algorithm started discounting them across the board.
The practical move: weave the tag into the sentence. Instead of #silverspringfood at the end, write “...at #romacucina, our #silverspring kitchen...” in the body. Same tag, ranked higher.
Move 5: Fill the alt-text field every time.

Instagram has an alt-text field on every post that almost nobody uses. It’s in the advanced settings under accessibility. The platform’s search algorithm and Google’s image crawler both read it. It’s a free keyword surface that 90% of restaurant accounts surrender by default.

The alt-text should describe the photo factually: “Hand-rolled pici pasta with traditional ragù, served at Roma Cucina, an Italian restaurant in Silver Spring, MD.” Plain language. The dish, the cuisine, the city. No emojis. The point is searchability, not personality.
What this changes about your week.

Not much, actually. The frequency stays the same. The photo budget stays the same. The fifteen seconds you used to spend writing “Made with love” becomes thirty seconds of writing the caption from the search box backward, plus ten seconds for the alt-text. Total added time per post: under a minute. Total added cost: zero.

What changes is what surfaces in search ninety days later. Save rate climbs first. Profile-click rate climbs second. Reservations climb a quarter behind that, because the people finding you on the search bar are deeper-funnel than the people finding you on the feed.

Don Goldstein manages two DMV restaurants and runs Muntin Digital . The 4.3x save lift cited here is the difference between two accounts he manages over the rolling 90-day window ending May 1, twenty twenty-six.

Key takeaways
Instagram truncates the caption at ~125 characters on the feed — that’s nine to fifteen words; bury the dish name later and the post is invisible to search.
Three entities per caption is the discipline: the dish (specific, not category), the cuisine, and the neighborhood.
Stacked hashtags at the bottom were penalized in Instagram’s late-twenty twenty-four update; two or three tags woven into the sentence outperform fifteen at the end.
Alt-text is searchable on both Instagram and Google; 90% of restaurant accounts skip the field and forfeit the surface free.
Likes don’t convert to bookings — saves and profile clicks do. Optimize captions for the metrics that actually move revenue.
